L303: ## 4. The Image of $\mathsf{Pop}$
L304: 
L305: Our goal in this section is to characterize the image of the pop-stack operator on the ornamentation lattice $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. This characterization, which we describe in cite66†Theorem 4.2 , is given by imposing a simple local criterion on each ornament in an ornamentation.
L306: Let $\mathsf{T}\in\mathrm{PT}_{n}$ and $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. For convenience, we add to $\mathsf{T}$ an extra imaginary node $\omega$, and we let $\delta(\omega)=\{\omega\}\cup\mathsf{T}$. We make the convention that $\omega$ is the parent of the root $\mathfrak{r}$ and that $\mathfrak{r}$ is the unique child of $\omega$. We impose that the ornament hung at $\omega$ is left unaffected by $\mathsf{Pop}$.
L307: As before, we say a node $v$ wraps a node $u$ in $\delta$ if $\delta(u)\subseteq\delta(v)$ and there does not exist a node $w$ such that $\delta(u)\subsetneq\delta(w)\subsetneq\delta(v)$. We then say that $v$ hugs $u$ in $\delta$ if $v$ wraps $u$ and there exists a child $u^{\prime}\in\mathrm{ch}_{\delta(u)}(u)$ such that $\Delta_{\delta(u)}(u^{\prime})=\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u^{\prime})$.
L308: Note that nodes whose ornaments are singletons can not be hugged, and that a node may be hugged by the imaginary node $\omega$ under our definition. We do not draw $\omega$ in diagrams.
L309: ###### Lemma 4.1.
L310: 
L311: Let $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. For any two nodes $u,v\in\mathsf{T}\cup\{\omega\}$, the ornaments $\delta(u)$ and $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta)(v)$ are either nested or disjoint.
L312: ###### Proof.
L313: If either $u$ or $v$ is the imaginary node $\omega$, then either $\delta(u)$ or $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta)(v)$ is $\mathsf{T}\cup\{\omega\}$, so the desired result is immediate. Thus, we may assume $u\neq\omega$ and $v\neq\omega$. By the definition of an ornamentation, $\delta(u)$ and $\delta(v)$ are either nested or disjoint, and by cite57†Lemma 2.6 , $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta)(v)\subseteq\delta(v)$.
L314: Thus, if $\delta(v)$ is disjoint from or contained in $\delta(u)$, then its subset $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta)(v)$ is also disjoint from or contained in $\delta(u)$. Now suppose $\delta(u)\subseteq\delta(v)$. There exists a node $v^{\prime}$ such that $\delta(u)\subseteq\delta(v^{\prime})\subseteq\delta(v)$ and such that $v$ wraps $v^{\prime}$ in $\delta$.
L315: Now, cite49†Lemma 2.3 implies that any minimal reduction $o$ of $\delta(v)$ will either contain or be disjoint from $\delta(v^{\prime})$, and hence will either contain or be disjoint from $\delta(u)$. According to cite51†Lemma 2.4 , $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta)(v)$ either contains or is disjoint from $\delta(u)$, as desired. ∎
L316: The following theorem is equivalent to cite42†Theorem 1.2 , but it is phrased using the language of hugs.
L317: ###### Theorem 4.2.
L318: 
L319: Let $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$. Then $\delta\in\mathsf{Pop}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}))$ if and only if each $u\in\mathsf{T}$ is not hugged in $\delta$ by any node in $\mathsf{T}\cup\{\omega\}$.
L320: ###### Proof.
L321: Suppose $\delta=\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{\prime})\in\mathsf{Pop}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}))$, and assume for the sake of contradiction that there exist $u\in\mathsf{T}$ and $v\in\mathsf{T}\cup\{\omega\}$ such that $v$ hugs $u$ in $\delta$. Since $v$ hugs $u$, there exists $u^{\prime}\in\mathrm{ch}_{\delta(u)}(u)$ such that $\Delta_{\delta(u)}(u^{\prime})=\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u^{\prime})$.
L322: cite57†Lemma 2.6 implies that $|\Delta_{\delta^{\prime}(u)}(u^{\prime})|>|\Delta_{\delta(u)}(u^{\prime})|=|\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u^{\prime})|$, so $\delta^{\prime}(u)\not\subseteq\delta(v)$. Additionally, $u^{\prime}\in\delta^{\prime}(u)\cap\delta(v)$ and $v\in\delta(v)\setminus\delta^{\prime}(u)$. Thus, $\delta^{\prime}(u)$ and $\delta(v)$ are neither disjoint nor nested. This contradicts cite67†Lemma 4.1 because $\delta(v)=\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{\prime})(v)$.
L323: To prove the converse, suppose now that each node $u\in\mathsf{T}$ is not hugged by any node in $\mathsf{T}\cup\{\omega\}$. For each $u\in\mathsf{T}$, let $\delta^{*}(u)=\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u)$, where $v\in\mathsf{T}\cup\{\omega\}$ is the unique node that wraps $u$ in $\delta$. We will show that $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})=\delta$. Fix $u\in\mathsf{T}$; we will show that $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)=\delta(u)$.
L324: Figure 6. An ornamentation $\delta$ and the ornamentation $\delta^{*}$ constructed in the proof of cite66†Theorem 4.2 .
L325: First, we show that $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)\subseteq\delta(u)$. Let $v$ be the node that wraps $u$ in $\delta$. Consider a node $w\not\in\delta(u)$; we wish to show that $w\not\in\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)$. If $w\not\in\delta^{*}(u)$, then this is immediate from cite57†Lemma 2.6 , so we may assume that $w\in\delta^{*}(u)\setminus\delta(u)$. Let $t$ be first node on the path from $u$ to $w$ that is not in $\delta(u)$. Then $w$ is a descendant of $t$, and $t$ must be a node wrapped by $v$ in $\delta$.
L326: It follows that $\delta^{*}(t)=\Delta_{\delta(v)}(t)$ and $\delta^{*}(u)=\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u)$, so $\delta^{*}(u)\setminus\delta^{*}(t)$ is a minimal reduction of $\delta^{*}(u)$. By part (iii) of cite51†Lemma 2.4 , this implies that $\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)$ is disjoint from $\delta^{*}(t)$. Since $w\leq_{\mathsf{T}}t<_{\mathsf{T}}u$ and $t\not\in\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)$, it follows that $w\not\in\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)$.
L327: Next, we show that $\delta(u)\subseteq\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)$. This is trivial if $\delta(u)=\{u\}$, so suppose $|\delta(u)|>1$. Let $w\in\delta(u)\setminus\{u\}$; we will show that $w\in\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)$. Let $u^{\prime}$ be the child of $u$ such that $w\leq_{\mathsf{T}}u^{\prime}$. Let $v$ be the node that wraps $u$ in $\delta$. Because $v$ does not hug $u$ by assumption, $\Delta_{\delta(u)}(u^{\prime})\subsetneq\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u^{\prime})$.
L328: Therefore, there is a node $u^{\prime\prime}\in\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u^{\prime})\setminus\Delta_{\delta(u)}(u^{\prime})$ that is wrapped by $v$ in $\delta$. By definition of $\delta^{*}$, we have $\delta^{*}(u)=\Delta_{\delta(v)}(u)$ and $\delta^{*}(u^{\prime})=\Delta_{\delta(u)}(u^{\prime})$, so $\delta^{*}(u^{\prime})$ contains $w$.
L329: It is not difficult to see that $u$ wraps $u^{\prime}$ and $u^{\prime\prime}$ in $\delta^{*}$, so $\delta^{*}(u^{\prime})$ and $\delta^{*}(u^{\prime\prime})$ are maximal subornaments of $\delta^{*}(u)$. Assume for the sake of contradiction that $w\not\in\mathsf{Pop}(\delta^{*})(u)$. By part (iii) of cite51†Lemma 2.4 , there exists a minimal reduction $o$ of $\delta^{*}(u)$ that does not contain $w$.
L330: By part (ii) of cite49†Lemma 2.3 , $o$ is a disjoint union of maximal subornaments of $\delta^{*}(u)$ not including $\delta^{*}(u^{\prime})$ (because it contains $w$) and not including $\delta^{*}(u^{\prime\prime})$ (as $u^{\prime\prime}$ is a descendant of $u^{\prime}$ and $o$ must be connected). But by part (iii) of cite49†Lemma 2.3 , this contradicts the minimality of $o$. ∎
L331: ## 5. The Image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$
L332: Now that we have characterized the image of $\mathsf{Pop}$ on an arbitrary ornamentation lattice, we turn to studying the images of higher iterates $\mathsf{Pop}$. This turns out to be much more complicated. cite43†Proposition 3.3 gives a necessary condition in terms of $v$-ranks for an ornamentation to lie in the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$. The $v$-ranks are fairly global, as determining the $v$-rank of a node could require checking every node in its subtree.
L333: We will provide another necessary (but not sufficient) condition for an ornamentation to lie in the image of $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}$, this time depending on features that are local to each ornament. We will then use this condition to completely characterize $\mathsf{Pop}^{k}(\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T}))$ when $\mathsf{T}$ is a chain (so $\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$ is a Tamari lattice).
L334: Let $\mathsf{T}\in\mathrm{PT}_{n}$ and $\delta\in\mathcal{O}(\mathsf{T})$, and fix a node $v\in\mathsf{T}$. Letting $\lambda_{v^{\prime}}$ be the $v^{\prime}$-section of $\delta(v)$ (for some $v^{\prime}\in\mathrm{ch}_{\delta(v)}(v)$), an ornament $\delta(u)\in\mathsf{T}$ is a bead of $\lambda_{v^{\prime}}$ in $\delta$ if $u\leq_{\mathsf{T}}v^{\prime}$, $u\not\in\delta(v)$, and for each node $w\in[v^{\prime},u]$, either $w\in\delta(v)$ or $\delta(w)$ is a singleton.
L335: (In particular, $\delta(u)$ must be a singleton to be a bead.)

L338: Let $\delta$ be the ornamentation of the tree $\mathsf{T}$ shown in cite68†Figure 7 . The ornament $\delta(t)$ has a section with $1$ bead and a section with $3$ beads. The ornaments $\delta(u)$ and $\delta(v)$ each have exactly one section, which has $3$ beads. The ornament $\delta(w)$ has one section with $4$ beads.

L200: ## 4 Connections between flips and sorting models
L201: 
L202: Our upper bounds in the previous section depend on bounds for sorting permutations. In this section, we study the connection in the other direction, showing that our lower bound on the diameter of the flip graph implies an $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound on the cost of sorting in various length-weighted sorting models.
L203: Sorting permutations of $[1..n]$ using a restricted set of operations has been widely studied. A main operation is the reversal of a subsequence. One of the earliest results of this kind was on “pancake” sorting [cite52†14 ], where a prefix of the sequence can be reversed. Bubble sort also fits into this model, as it operates by swapping two adjacent elements at a time, which is a reversal of size two.
L204: The number of size-two reversals it makes is equal to the number of inversions of the permutation and is $\Theta(n^{2})$ in the worst case. More generally, any permutation can be sorted with $\Theta(n)$ reversals [cite53†19 ] if arbitrarily large reversals are allowed. Most of the results until now have been about the number of operations required.
L205: Recently, Pinter and Skiena [cite54†23 ] formulated a model that allows reversals of any size, but assigns them a cost proportional to the length of the reversed subsequence. This model has applications in comparative genomics, where it models a sequence of mutations in the evolution of a chromosome. Bender et al. [cite55†2 ] showed that any input sequence can be sorted in this model with worst-case cost $O(n\log^{2}n)$, and gave an $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound.
L206: Figure 7: An illustration of the swaps permitted in the contiguous reversals model (left), the non-contiguous reversals model (middle), and the non-crossing swaps model (right).
L207: We present a more general length-weighted sorting model, based on swaps. Given a permutation $\rho$, pick an interval $[i..j]$ with $1\leq i<j\leq n$ and $j-i=k$ and perform a set of swaps in it. The cost of this operation is $O(k)$. Adding constraints on the kinds of swaps allowed inside the interval leads to more specific models (see Figure cite56†7 ):

L209: Contiguous reversals
L210: 
L211: 
L212: Reverse the entire interval $[i..j]$.
L213: 
L214: Non-contiguous reversals
L215: Pick a subsequence $i_{1},\ldots,i_{m}$ of $[i..j]$ and reverse its elements, without changing the position of any element outside the subsequence.
L216: 
L217: Non-crossing swaps
L218: 
L219: 
L220: Swap a set $\{(i_{1},j_{1}),\ldots,(i_{m},j_{m})\}$ of pairs inside $[i..j]$ such that there do not exist $x,y\in[1..m]$ with $x<y$ for which $i_{x}\leq i_{y}\leq j_{x}\leq j_{y}$, i.e, either the two intervals $[i_{x},j_{x}]$ and $[i_{y},j_{y}]$ nest or they are disjoint.
L221: To the best of our knowledge, the latter two models are novel. Of the three models presented, the non-crossing swaps model is the most general, as it can simulate both other models. In fact, the non-crossing swaps model is more general than (length-weighted versions of) a large number of sorting models [cite57†12 , Chapter 3].
L222: We use our results on flips to give an $\Omega(n\log n)$ lower bound on the worst-case cost of sorting in the non-crossing swaps model and therefore in all of the sorting models that can be simulated by it. Note that our proof of Theorem cite43†1 can be interpreted as an $O(n\log n)$ upper bound on the cost of sorting in the non-contiguous reversals model, and thereby also in the non-crossing swaps model. We first show how to simulate a non-crossing swap with flips.
L223: The proof is very similar to the proof of Lemma cite42†1 .
L224: ###### Lemma 3.
L225: 
L226: Let $\rho$ and $\rho^{\prime}$ be two permutations of $[1..n]$ such that $\rho^{\prime}$ can be obtained from $\rho$ using one set of non-crossing swaps in an interval of length $k$. Then the canonical triangulation $(T^{*},\rho)$ can be flipped to $(T^{*},\rho^{\prime})$ with $O(k)$ flips.
L227: ###### Proof.
L228: 
L229: Let $S=[i..j]$ be the sequence of edges in which we perform the swaps. We proceed by induction on $|S|$. In the base case, $|S|=0$ and we are done, so let $|S|=k$ and assume that the lemma holds for all $|S|<k$. If there is an edge $e$ in $S$ that is not involved in any swap, we flip it. This results in a smaller convex polygon and reduces $|S|$ by one, so we can perform the swaps there by induction and flip $e$ back afterwards.
L230: If every edge is involved in a swap, consider a swap $x=(i_{x},j_{x})$ such that no other swap is nested inside $x$. The edges $i_{x}$ and $j_{x}$ must be consecutive, since all edges are involved in some swap, and swaps do not cross. Thus, they form a convex pentagon and can be swapped with five flips, as shown in Figure cite41†2 . But instead of completing this swap sequence, we halt it after the first three flips.
L231: This leaves the edges $i_{x}$ and $j_{x}$ out of the way of the remaining edges, so we can perform the rest of the swaps by induction. Afterwards, we perform the final two flips to return $i_{x}$ and $j_{x}$. Thus, we can perform each swap with 5 flips, giving a total cost of $O(k)$. ∎
L232: Combining this lemma with Theorem cite58†3 gives the desired lower bound.
L233: ###### Theorem 6.
L234: 
L235: The worst-case cost of sorting a permutation of $[1..n]$ in the non-crossing swaps model is $\Omega(n\log n)$.
L236: ## 5 Spiral polygons
L237: 
L238: In this section, we prove the Orbit Conjecture for spiral polygons, even when there are multiple orbits. We provide a complete characterization of the orbits, and prove a tight quadratic bound on the diameter of each connected component of the flip graph. Finally, we show how to test for the condition of the Orbit Conjecture in linear time.
L239: A vertex of a polygon is a convex vertex if the interior angle at the vertex is less than $\pi$, otherwise it is reflex. A spiral polygon is a polygon in which all reflex vertices are consecutive along the boundary.
L240: For a spiral polygon $P$ with $m$ convex and $k$ reflex vertices, let $C=c_{1}c_{2}\ldots c_{m}$ denote the convex chain in clockwise order and $R=r_{1}r_{2}\ldots r_{k}$ denote the reflex chain in counterclockwise order such that $c_{1}$ and $r_{1}$ are adjacent, and $c_{m}$ and $r_{k}$ are adjacent. For any vertex $c$ on the convex chain (resp. reflex chain), let $V(c)$ be the set of vertices on the reflex chain (resp. convex chain) that are visible from $c$.

L246: Consider a triangulated 5-vertex polygon with a single reflex vertex (see Figure cite59†8(a) ). The two diagonals cannot be swapped with flips, thereby implying that the flip graph is disconnected. The same thing happens with any spiral polygon with only 3 convex vertices—there is a unique triangulation and the flip graph is either a singleton (if there is at most one reflex vertex), or disconnected. We now characterize when the flip graph is connected.
L247: We only consider spiral polygons with at least 4 convex vertices. A spiral polygon is locally convex if it has at least four convex vertices and for every four consecutive vertices $a$, $b$, $c$, and $d$ on the convex chain, the quadrilateral $abcd$ is empty. Note that it is possible for four consecutive convex vertices to form a non-convex quadrilateral, but then the quadrilateral cannot be empty. Local convexity is the key to the characterization of the orbits and connectivity of the flip graph.
L248: ###### Theorem 7.
L249: 
L250: For an $n$-vertex spiral polygon $\mathcal{P}$ with at least 4 convex vertices the flip graph, $FG_{\mathcal{P}}$, is connected if and only if $\mathcal{P}$ is locally convex. Furthermore, the diameter of each connected component of $FG_{\mathcal{P}}$ is $O(n^{2})$.
L251: 
L252: We start by showing that if $\mathcal{P}$ is locally convex, then its flip graph is connected. Observe the following:
L253: ###### Lemma 4.
L254: 
L255: If $\mathcal{P}$ is locally convex, then for any two consecutive vertices $r_{i},r_{i+1}\in R$ on the reflex chain, $|V(r_{i})\cap V(r_{i+1})|\geq 3$.
L256: ###### Proof.
L257: 
L258: Extend the segment $r_{i},r_{i+1}$ in both directions until it hits the convex chain and exits the polygon. Let $c_{j},\ldots,c_{j^{\prime}}$ be the vertices of the convex chain between these two exit points, noting that $j>1$ and $j^{\prime}<m$. Observe that $V(r_{i})\cap V(r_{i+1})=\{c_{j},\ldots,c_{j^{\prime}}\}$.
L259: Suppose that $|V(r_{i})\cap V(r_{i+1})|\leq 2$. We will show that $\mathcal{P}$ is not locally convex. Consider the vertices $c_{j-1},c_{j},\ldots,c_{j^{\prime}},c_{j^{\prime}+1}$. They form a quadrilateral or triangle that contains $r_{i}$ and $r_{i+1}$. If they form a quadrilateral, this violates local convexity, and if they form a triangle then we can extend it to a quadrilateral that violates local convexity. ∎
L260: To prove connectivity of the flip graph, we define the following canonical triangulation $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$, together with a partition of its diagonals into fans. The canonical triangulation will be defined by specifying the triangle incident to each edge of the polygon. Let $r_{i}r_{i+1}$ be an edge of the reflex chain with $V(r_{i})\cap V(r_{i+1})=\{c_{j},\ldots,c_{j^{\prime}}\}$. The apex of the triangle on edge $r_{i}r_{i+1}$ is defined to be $c_{\left\lfloor(j+j^{\prime})/2\right\rfloor}$.
L261: The diagonals of all such triangles incident to a given convex vertex $c$ constitute the convex fan at $c$. See Figure cite60†9(a) . After this, each edge $c_{j}c_{j+1}$ has a unique reflex vertex that can be its apex. We add these triangles to $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$.
